newsitem.title: FRANCE: Baby escapes as rebels slay 31 in Algeria massacre.
newsitem.headline: Baby escapes as rebels slay 31 in Algeria massacre.

text.p: Moslem fundamentalists slaughtered 31 people, slitting their throats between Tuesday night and Wednesday morning, in one of the bloodiest attacks on an Algerian village in five years of violence.
Algerian security forces said simply that 31 people died. But eyewitness survivors and relatives of the dead who visited the village on Wednesday said all had had their throats cut.
Among those slaughtered was a newly-married man and his bride, and 10 other women.
"He was slaughtered on the steps of his home after opening the door, and his newly-wed wife was killed in their bed," said one witness contacted by telephone.

Three children had a close escape, witnesses said. A baby of 18 months lay asleep in his cot, apparently overlooked by the killers. Two other children, aged eight and 10, fled into the mountains with other villagers.
The 31 dead, who belonged to five families, included elderly women, one of whom was aged at least 80. They are to be buried on Thursday.
One relative said those who survived planned to abandon their village forever after the burials.
"We don't know why the families were targeted. Only one family has, we believe, a relative in the armed forces doing his military service," he added.
The security forces in a statement on the official Algerian news agency APS, said 31 people had been "assassinated in a cowardly way" in what it described as "this ignoble terrorist act".

The raid took place on Sid el Kebir, on the road to Chrea in Blida province, 50 km (30 miles) south of Algiers. The village is the site of a Zaouia, a traditional religious centre of someone locally respected for piety or learning.
Interior Minister Mustapha Ben Mansour condemned the attack, the second in three nights. At the weekend, 13 people had their throats cut in another attack.
Neither official source gave details, but the phrase "in a cowardly way" has been used in Algeria to describe the cold-blooded killing of victims by cutting their throats.
Algeria uses the term "terrorist" to describe Moslem rebels who have been fighting since 1992 to topple the government.

Ben Mansour said the dead were civilians: "In targeting once again defenceless people, these criminals only confirm the baseness and unqualified cowardice which drives them in their determination to assassinate, without distinction and with ignoble savagery, peaceful citizens."
An estimated 50,000 people have been killed since violence erupted following the authorities' cancellation in January 1992 of a general election dominated by Islamic fundamentalists.
In a chilling statement published last Sunday, Algeria's most ruthless Islamist movement, the Armed Islamic Group (GIA), dismissed outrage at the deaths of civilians.
"There are many religious proofs which make legitimate (our) bombing operations even when there are civilian victims," it said.
